title: How Do You Open a Business Bank Account for an LLC?
summary: How to open a business bank account for an LLC: why it protects your liability shield, the documents you need (EIN, articles, operating agreement), the step-by-step process, and how to choose a bank.
body_markdown:
Forming an LLC gives you a liability shield, but a separate bank account is what keeps it intact. Running business money through your personal account, or the reverse, is one of the fastest ways to weaken that protection.


A dedicated business account isn't just tidy; it's part of what makes the LLC do its job.


This guide covers why your LLC needs its own account, the documents banks require, how to open one step by step, how to choose a bank, and how to keep business and personal money truly separate.


## Why your LLC needs its own bank account


The most important reason is legal. An LLC works by separating your personal assets from the business's debts and liabilities. Mixing personal and business money, what courts call commingling, can let someone "pierce the corporate veil" and come after your personal assets. A separate account is the clearest evidence that the LLC is a distinct entity.


Beyond protection, a business account makes everything else easier. Your bookkeeping is cleaner when every transaction in the account is a business transaction, tax time is simpler, and you can build business credit separate from your personal credit.


It also just looks professional. Getting paid into, and paying from, an account in your business's name signals to clients and vendors that they're dealing with a real company.


## What you need to open the account


Banks legally can't open a business account without proof the LLC exists and a tax ID, so gather these before you apply.


Document Why the Bank Needs It


EIN (Employer Identification Number) Your LLC's federal tax ID


Articles of Organization Proof the LLC legally exists


Operating Agreement Shows ownership and who can act for the LLC


Government-issued photo ID Verifies the owners and signers


Beneficial ownership details Verification of the individuals behind the LLC


The EIN is the one people forget. It's free from the IRS, and you can[get an EIN online](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/get-an-employer-identification-number-ein) in minutes.


A single-member LLC can sometimes open an account with the owner's SSN, but an EIN is cleaner and keeps your personal number off business paperwork. Some banks also want a business licence if your industry requires one.


## How to open the account


With your documents ready, the process is usually quick, often under 30 minutes online. Follow these steps.


1. **Form the LLC first.** The LLC must be legally registered before you can open an account in its name. Our guide on[how to incorporate](https://www.finlens.app/blogs/how-to-incorporate) covers forming the entity.
2. **Get your EIN.** Apply free through the IRS if you don't already have one.
3. **Choose a bank.** Compare traditional and online banks on fees, features, and fit, covered below.
4. **Gather your documents.** Have the EIN, formation documents, operating agreement, and ID in hand, digitally and on paper.
5. **Complete the application.** Apply online or in a branch, entering the LLC and beneficial owner details.
6. **Fund the account.** Make the opening deposit, often as little as $25 to $100.
7. **Set up access.** Decide who can sign for the LLC, per your operating agreement, and set up debit cards and online banking.


Once it's open and funded, route all business income and expenses through it from day one.


## Online vs traditional banks


There's no single right answer, just a trade-off. Traditional banks offer branches, in-person help, cash deposits, and often broader services like lending and merchant accounts. If your business handles cash or you value a local relationship, a traditional bank fits.


Online banks and fintech providers usually win on fees and convenience. Many offer no monthly fees, no minimums, and slick apps, though cash deposits can be harder and some aren't banks themselves but work with partner banks. Confirm your funds are FDIC-insured either way.


For most digital-first LLCs, an online business account is enough. For cash-heavy or lending-dependent businesses, a traditional bank earns its place.


## What to compare before you choose


A few factors separate a good account from an expensive one. Look at monthly fees and how to waive them, transaction and deposit limits, and any minimum balance requirements.


Then weigh the practical fit: FDIC insurance, whether the account earns interest, and how easily it connects to your accounting software. That last one matters more than people expect, since a clean bank feed into your books saves hours of manual entry every month.


Also consider room to grow. The account you open today should still work as the business scales, so factor in lending, merchant services, and multi-user access even if you don't need them yet.


## Keeping business and personal separate


Opening the account is step one; the discipline is keeping the line clean afterward. The liability protection and the clean books both depend on never mixing the two.


That means paying yourself deliberately, as an[owner's draw](https://www.finlens.app/blogs/how-to-record-owners-draw) or salary, rather than dipping into the business account for personal spending. It means running every business expense through the business account or card and keeping personal purchases out of it entirely.


This is also where the account pays off in your books. When every transaction in the account is a business transaction, your[LLC bookkeeping](https://www.finlens.app/blogs/llc-bookkeeping-software) is dramatically simpler.


[Finlens](https://www.finlens.app/founders) connects to that account and keeps categorisation and reconciliation current, so the separation you maintain in banking flows into clean books, without the[DIY cleanup](https://www.finlens.app/blogs/the-hidden-cost-of-diy-accounting-for-small-businesses) that commingling creates.


## Common mistakes


The costliest mistake is skipping the separate account entirely and running the LLC through a personal one, which undermines the liability shield and tangles your books. It's the exact thing an LLC is supposed to prevent.


Others include showing up without the right documents, usually the EIN confirmation or operating agreement, which delays the application by weeks, and treating the business account like a personal wallet after opening it. Choosing an account with high fees you could have avoided is a smaller but common one.


Each of these is easy to sidestep with preparation. Form the entity, get the EIN, bring the documents, and keep the account strictly for business.


## Conclusion


Opening a business bank account for an LLC is a simple task with an outsized payoff. It protects the liability shield you formed the LLC for, keeps your bookkeeping clean, and lets you build business credit, all from one straightforward setup.


Do the prep and it goes smoothly: form the LLC, get your EIN, gather your formation documents and ID, and pick a bank that fits how you operate. Then fund the account and route everything business through it.


The real work starts after you open it. Keep business and personal money strictly separate, and both your legal protection and your books stay intact. That discipline, more than the account itself, is what makes the LLC structure actually deliver.


## Frequently asked questions


### What documents do I need to open a business bank account for an LLC?


Most banks require your EIN, Articles of Organization, an operating agreement (especially for multi-member LLCs), and a government-issued photo ID for the owners. Many also ask for beneficial ownership details and, in some industries, a business licence. Requirements vary by bank, so confirm the exact list before you apply.


### Do I need an EIN to open an LLC bank account?


Usually, yes. Multi-member LLCs and any LLC with employees need an EIN, and most banks require one. A single-member LLC can sometimes open an account with the owner's SSN, but getting an EIN is free from the IRS, keeps your personal number off business paperwork, and is generally recommended.


### Why does my LLC need a separate bank account?


A separate account preserves the LLC's liability protection by keeping business and personal finances distinct. Mixing them, called commingling, can let a court disregard the LLC and reach your personal assets. It also keeps your bookkeeping clean, simplifies taxes, and helps you build business credit.


### Can I use my personal bank account for my LLC?


You can technically, but you shouldn't. Running an LLC through a personal account weakens the liability shield the LLC provides and tangles your business and personal transactions, making bookkeeping and taxes much harder. A dedicated business account is one of the first things to set up after forming an LLC.


### How long does it take to open a business bank account?


If you have the documents ready, an online application often takes under 30 minutes, and some accounts open the same day. LLCs and corporations may need extra verification, which can add a few days. Missing documents, especially the EIN or operating agreement, are the usual cause of delays.


### Should I use an online bank or a traditional bank for my LLC?


It depends on your needs. Traditional banks offer branches, cash deposits, and broader services like lending. Online banks and fintech providers often have lower fees and better apps but can make cash deposits harder. Digital-first businesses usually do well online; cash-heavy or lending-dependent ones may prefer a traditional bank.


### How much money do I need to open a business bank account?


Many business checking accounts open with a small deposit, often $25 to $100, and some have no minimum at all. Others require a higher balance to waive monthly fees. Check the specific account's terms, since opening requirements and ongoing balance rules vary widely between banks.


### Do single-member LLCs need a business bank account?


Yes. Even a single-member LLC benefits from a separate account, because the same liability protection depends on keeping business and personal money apart. Running a single-member LLC out of a personal account is one of the most common ways owners accidentally weaken their limited liability.
